candidate.answerReason: The common logarithm value gives \(q^2=p(p+q)\), using \(12^2=9\cdot16\). Thus the positive ratio \(r=q/p\) satisfies \(r^2-r-1=0\), whose only positive root is the value in choice D.

methods.label: Introduce the common exponent
methods.explanation:
Equal logarithms give a common exponent. The useful relation among the bases is \(12^2=9\cdot16\), which will eliminate that exponent.

Let the common logarithm value be the real number \(t\). By the definition of logarithms,
\[
p=9^t,\qquad q=12^t,\qquad p+q=16^t.
\]
All bases are positive, so the laws of real powers apply. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
q^2&=(12^t)^2=(12^2)^t\\
&=(9\cdot16)^t=9^t16^t\\
&=p(p+q).
\end{aligned}
\]
We want the ratio rather than the individual numbers. Set \(r=q/p\), which is positive because \(p,q>0\). Dividing the last equation by the nonzero number \(p^2\) gives
\[
r^2=1+r,
\qquad\text{or}\qquad r^2-r-1=0.
\]
The quadratic formula yields
\[
r=\frac{1\pm\sqrt5}{2}.
\]
The minus-sign root is negative and cannot equal \(q/p\). Hence
\[
\frac qp=\boxed{\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).

The method uses logarithms as exponents directly, then exploits the base relation with real exponent laws. The quadratic formula is local to this route, and positivity selects the admissible root.

review.mathematicalCheck: The common exponent and \(12^2=9\cdot16\) give \(q^2=p(p+q)\). Since \(p>0\), division by \(p^2\) yields \(r^2=r+1\) for \(r=q/p>0\). Its only positive root is \((1+\sqrt5)/2\), choice D.
